They will later connect those facts to the myths and to Rick Riordan's modern adaptation.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students compare myths across texts and analyze cultural values. Today's inference work with clues of fear, hope, and values begins that analysis and builds curiosity about the myths."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"myth","definition":"a traditional story, often about gods, heroes, or nature, that a culture tells to explain the world or share its beliefs","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"mythology","definition":"a collection of myths from a particular culture; also the study of myths","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"infer","definition":"to figure something out by combining clues in the text with what you already know","tier":"support"},{"word":"culture","definition":"the beliefs, customs, and stories shared by a group of people","tier":"support"},{"word":"annotate","definition":"to mark a text with notes, underlines, and questions as you read","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"What Are Myths?","author":"Newsela Staff","pages":"Full article"},{"title":"Prometheus and Pandora myths (three short unlabeled passages)","author":"Coolidge","pages":"Three passages selected by the teacher"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students read \"What Are Myths?\" and discuss initial ideas about why cultures create stories about gods, nature, danger, or the unknown, and record a first definition of myth.","activities":[{"id":"launch-read-discuss","title":"Read and Discuss: What Are Myths?","minutes":15,"standards":["RI.6.4","SL.6.1.a"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"What Are Myths?","pages":"Full article"},{"type":"directions","text":"Read \"What Are Myths?\" Underline one sentence that helps explain why people tell myths. Then use Turn and Talk to share it with a partner. On your own paper, write your first definition of *myth* in one sentence. Save it for later."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today we start a unit about stories that are thousands of years old. Before we meet them, let's find out what you already think a myth is."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"According to the article, why do cultures create stories about gods, nature, danger, or the unknown?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"People didn't have science, so they made stories to explain things like storms or why the sun rises. The stories helped them feel less afraid of things they couldn't control."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Point to a sentence in the article that supports your idea. What does it tell us?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The article says myths explained things people couldn't understand, like thunder. That shows myths were a way to make sense of scary or mysterious things."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"As we read, I'll use the word *myth* in context. In this article, a myth is a traditional story that a culture tells to explain the world or share its beliefs. Check how the article uses the word as you reread."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Keep this quick. Collect two or three ideas on the board under the heading \"Why do cultures make myths?\" Students will return to these after the passages. Accept any reasonable idea tied to the article."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Hold on to your first definition. We will test it against some real ancient stories in a moment."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Students infer meaning from three unlabeled passages of Coolidge's Prometheus/Pandora myths, annotating evidence in small groups, then share theories and learn the morphology of mythology and the source of the passages.","activities":[{"id":"lia-mystery-passages","title":"Mystery Passages: Annotate and Infer","minutes":15,"standards":["RI.6.1","RI.6.4","SL.6.1.a"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"Three unlabeled passages from Coolidge's Prometheus/Pandora myths","pages":"Teacher-selected short passages, with no title or author shown"},{"type":"directions","text":"In your group, read the three passages. You will not be told where they come from. Annotate each passage: underline words and phrases that are clues, and write notes in the margin. Then answer together: (1) What problem is this passage trying to explain? (2) What kind of world does this story imagine? (3) What clues hint at fear, hope, or cultural values? Use evidence from the text in every answer."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"You are detectives today. You have no title, no author, and no background. All you have are the words on the page. Everything you say needs a clue."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What problem is this passage trying to explain?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"This passage seems to explain why people have to work hard and suffer. The words about trouble and sorrow spreading across the earth are the clue."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What kind of world does this story imagine?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A world where gods are powerful and watch humans. The gods can punish people and give gifts, so the story imagines gods controlling human lives."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What clues hint at fear, hope, or cultural values?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The word hope stays behind when everything else escapes, so people in this culture valued hope. Words about punishment hint at fear of angry gods."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"When you read a word you're not sure about, use the words around it as clues. Say the unfamiliar word, look at nearby words, and ask what meaning would make sense in this sentence."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Choose short passages: one about Prometheus giving fire, one about Pandora's jar or box opening, and one about what remained inside. Remove names and titles if possible. Circulate and push students from vague answers to specific words. Ask, \"Which words told you that?\""},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely and using expanded noun phrases to describe clues and ideas from the passages.","sayAsk":"Model: \"The word ___ suggests ___.\" \"This passage imagines a world where ___.\" Expand nouns: \"gods\" becomes \"powerful, watchful gods\"; \"trouble\" becomes \"terrible trouble that spreads across the earth.\" Let students point to the clue before speaking and talk in their home language first if helpful.","watchFor":"If a student only names the topic, then prompt: \"Which words in the passage show that?\" If a student gives a clue without meaning, then prompt: \"Add: This suggests ___.\" Success: students cite a word or phrase and explain what it hints about fear, hope, or values, using at least one expanded noun phrase."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RI.6.1"],"stem":"A group reads a passage in which every trouble escapes from a jar, but one thing stays inside. Which inference is best supported by the text?","choices":[{"text":"The story imagines a world in which troubles are part of life, but hope remains.","correct":true,"rationale":"Correct. The trouble escaping and the one thing staying behind are both clues to this larger idea."},{"text":"The story is a set of instructions for storing things in jars.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. The jar is a story element that carries meaning, not a practical lesson on storage."},{"text":"The story shows that the culture had no fears.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. Troubles spreading across the world shows people feared hardship and suffering."},{"text":"The story is only about one character's bad day.","correct":false,"rationale":"Incorrect. The troubles spread to all people, so the story explains something about the whole world."}]}]},{"id":"lia-share-reveal","title":"Share Theories and Reveal the Source","minutes":15,"standards":["L.6.4.b","RI.6.4","SL.6.1","SL.6.1.a"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Share one theory from your group about what the passages are and where they might come from. Listen to other groups and build on their ideas. Then return to your first definition of *myth* and add to it using evidence from the passages."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What is your group's theory? What evidence led you there?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"We think these are ancient stories that explain why the world has suffering. We noticed gods, a gift to humans, and a jar of troubles. Those are clues that it's a made-up story to explain something real."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Now for the reveal. These passages come from Coolidge's retellings of the myths of Prometheus and Pandora, ancient Greek stories. Prometheus is the god who gave fire to humans, and Pandora is the woman who opened the jar."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Look at the word *mythology*. It breaks into *myth* plus *logy*. The Greek root *logy* means \"study of.\" So *mythology* means the study of myths, and we also use it for a culture's collection of myths. Compare *bio* plus *logy*: *bio* means life, so *biology* is the study of life."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using what you know about the root *logy*, what might *geology* or *zoology* mean?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Geology would be the study of the earth, because geo means earth. Zoology would be the study of animals, since zoo is about animals."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How would you improve your first definition of *myth* now?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A myth is an old story from a culture that explains something about the world, like why people suffer, and shows what the people feared and valued."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Have students add to their original definition in a different color or below the first one, so growth is visible. Do not teach plot details beyond the reveal; Lesson 2 builds background knowledge."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Help students evaluate language choices and use morphology to define mythology while expanding noun phrases when revising their definition.","sayAsk":"Frames: \"I think the passages are ___ because ___.\" \"The root logy means ___, so mythology means ___.\" \"A myth is a ___ story that ___.\" Show bio + logy and myth + logy on the board with color-coded parts. Offer a word bank: explain, fear, hope, gods, ancient.","watchFor":"If a student can name the parts but not the meaning, then prompt: \"What does each part mean? Put them together.\" If a revised definition is a single short noun, then prompt: \"Add a describing word or a who-or-what phrase.\" Success: students define mythology using the root and revise their definition of myth with at least one expanded noun phrase."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Making inferences from the passages","tryThis":"Provide a clue-to-meaning chart with columns \"Clue (word or phrase)\", \"What it makes me think\", and \"Because...\". Model one row, then have students complete a second together."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Analyzing cultural values","tryThis":"Ask: Which passage tells you the most about what the culture valued, and why? How might a different culture explain the same problem differently?"}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how their understanding of myths has changed.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-quick-write","title":"Quick Write: What Is a Myth Now?","minutes":5,"standards":["RI.6.1","L.6.4.b"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write a few sentences: What is a myth, and what did the mystery passages show about the people who told these stories? Use at least one clue from a passage and the word *mythology*."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What did one clue from the passages tell you about what ancient people feared or valued?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"A myth is an old story that explains something about the world. In the passage, hope stayed in the jar after the troubles escaped, which shows the culture valued hope. Studying myths, or mythology, helps us understand people's beliefs."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework","purpose":"Optional independent reading and reflection.","activities":[{"id":"homework-independent-reading","title":"Independent Reading and Myth Hunt","minutes":0,"standards":["RI.6.1"],"routine":"Independent Reading","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read your independent reading book for 20 minutes and record the date, pages, and one or two sentences in your reading log. Optional: think of a story you know that explains something in nature (like why the sky has thunder) and write one sentence about it."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students read \"What Are Myths?\" to form first ideas about why cultures create myths, then annotate three unlabeled Coolidge passages to infer problems explained, imagined worlds, and clues about fear, hope, and values. The reveal of the Prometheus/Pandora source and the root logy in mythology leads students to revise their definition of myth.","keyActivities":["Read and Discuss: What Are Myths?","Mystery Passages: Annotate and Infer","Share Theories and Reveal the Source","Quick Write: What Is a Myth Now?"],"vocabularyTaught":["myth","mythology","infer","culture","annotate"],"standardsCovered":["L.6.4.b","RI.6.1","RI.6.4","SL.6.1.a","SL.6.1"]}}
